chunks.subject: AP English Literature
chunks.title: Literary Argument — Row A: Thesis (0–1)
chunks.content: AP English Literature Literary Argument, Row A Thesis (0–1 points). 1 point: responds to the prompt with a thesis that presents a defensible interpretation of the selected work — i.e. a defensible claim about the impact of a memory on a character, or how that impact contributes to an interpretation of the work as a whole. 0 points: no defensible thesis; only restates the prompt; or a generalized comment about the work that doesn't respond to the prompt. Any reasonable interpretation of 'the impact of a memory' is acceptable. The thesis may be multiple sentences in close proximity and appear anywhere.

chunks.subject: AP English Literature
chunks.title: Literary Argument — Row B: Evidence & Commentary (0–4)
chunks.content: AP English Literature Literary Argument, Row B Evidence AND Commentary (0–4 points). 0: restates thesis, repeats info, or irrelevant. 1: mostly general evidence focused on narrative/plot description rather than specifics; commentary only summarizes. 2: some specific relevant evidence; commentary explains how some evidence relates to the argument, but no line of reasoning or it is faulty. 3: specific evidence supporting all claims in a line of reasoning; commentary explains how some evidence supports it. 4: specific evidence for all claims; commentary consistently explains how the evidence supports a line of reasoning. To earn the 4th point the response must address the interpretation of the selected work AS A WHOLE. Grammatical errors that interfere with communication cannot earn the 4th point. (Note: unlike the poetry/prose rows, this row does NOT require explaining literary techniques.)

chunks.subject: AP English Literature
chunks.title: Literary Argument — Row C: Sophistication (0–1)
chunks.content: AP English Literature Literary Argument, Row C Sophistication (0–1 points). 1 point: demonstrates sophistication of thought and/or develops a complex literary argument by any of: identifying and exploring complexities or tensions within the selected work; situating the interpretation in a broader context; accounting for alternative interpretations; or employing a consistently vivid and persuasive style. Does NOT earn the point for sweeping generalizations, only hinting at other readings, oversimplifying, or ineffective complex language. Must be part of the argument, not merely a phrase.

chunks.subject: AP English Literature
chunks.title: Literary Argument exemplar — Sample 3A, score 1-4-1 (6/6)
chunks.content: Literary Argument (A Tale of Two Cities) scored 6/6 (Thesis 1, Evidence & Commentary 4, Sophistication 1). Thesis (1): defensible interpretation that memory's impact is seen chiefly through Dr. Manette, reflecting both individual trauma and the fate of Paris. Evidence & Commentary (4): specific evidence for all claims (shoe-making obsession; ties to the Revolution; parallels to the DeFarges) with commentary consistently supporting a thoughtful line of reasoning about memory driving conflict and growth, addressing the work as a whole. Sophistication (1): situates the interpretation in a broader context — Manette as a smaller-scale representation of an entire populace's sorrow.

chunks.subject: AP English Literature
chunks.title: Literary Argument exemplar — Sample 3B, score 1-3-0 (4/6)
chunks.content: Literary Argument (The Leavers) scored 4/6 (Thesis 1, Evidence & Commentary 3, Sophistication 0). Thesis (1): defensible interpretation that Deming's memory symbolizes the effects of parental absence on a child's growth. Evidence & Commentary (3): specific evidence for claims (becoming the 'outsider'; Chinese identity and Fuzhou language) with commentary — but the identity-struggle evidence is not adequately explained, so short of 4. Sophistication (0): attempts a broader context of parental absence but asserts the connection as fact rather than developing it.

chunks.subject: AP English Literature
chunks.title: Literary Argument exemplar — Sample 3C, score 1-2-0 (3/6)
chunks.content: Literary Argument (Frankenstein) scored 3/6 (Thesis 1, Evidence & Commentary 2, Sophistication 0). Thesis (1): defensible interpretation that memories drive Frankenstein's poor decisions until he seems monstrous himself. Evidence & Commentary (2): some specific relevant evidence (disgust at the creature; refusal to confess) but no commentary connecting the first piece to a claim, and the progression between claims is not explained, so no clear line of reasoning; ends with a simplistic explanation. Sophistication (0): not demonstrated.
